hints: Focus on the conditions and structures in each statement, aqueous versus alcoholic NaOH, C-Cl versus C-Br, and primary versus tertiary carbon.
Remember that aqueous NaOH favours substitution to an alcohol, C-Br breaks more easily than C-Cl, and a tertiary halogenoalkane strongly favours SN1.
Compare the two carbocations by counting alkyl groups around the positive carbon, more alkyl groups means more stabilisation by induction and hyperconjugation.
walkthrough:
**Check statement A: substitution or elimination?**

Think about what aqueous NaOH does. Aqueous conditions favour nucleophilic substitution to form an alcohol.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{NaBr}$$
Ethene by elimination needs hot ethanolic NaOH, so ethene is not the major product here.

**Check statement B: which halogen leaves faster?**

Reactivity depends on bond strength and leaving group ability. The $\text{C-Br}$ bond is weaker and longer than the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond.

$$\text{bond strength: C-Cl > C-Br, so Br}^- \text{ leaves more easily}$$
So 1-bromobutane reacts more rapidly than 1-chlorobutane, the statement is reversed.

**Check statement C: SN1 or SN2 for a tertiary bromide?**

Look at $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_3\text{CBr}$. The carbon attached to Br is attached to three other carbons, so it is tertiary.

$$\text{tertiary halogenoalkane + bulky groups = SN1 favoured, SN2 blocked}$$
Hydrolysis occurs mostly by SN1 via a stable tertiary carbocation, not SN2.

**Check statement D: compare carbocation stability**

$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$ is a primary carbocation with one alkyl group. $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$ is a tertiary carbocation with three methyl groups.

$$\text{stability: tertiary > secondary > primary}$$
Alkyl groups donate electron density by the inductive effect and hyperconjugation, so the tertiary ion is much more stable. This statement is correct.

options.A: False. Aqueous NaOH gives nucleophilic substitution to ethanol as the major product. Elimination to ethene is favoured by hot ethanolic NaOH, not aqueous NaOH.
options.B: False. Bromide is a better leaving group than chloride because the C-Br bond is weaker than the C-Cl bond. So 1-bromobutane reacts more rapidly than 1-chlorobutane at the same temperature.
options.C: False. (C2H5)3CBr is a tertiary bromoalkane. It is sterically hindered to SN2 attack and forms a stable tertiary carbocation, so hydrolysis goes mostly by SN1, not SN2.
options.D: Correct. The primary butyl cation has only one alkyl group stabilising the positive charge, while the tert-butyl cation has three methyl groups. Greater inductive donation and hyperconjugation make (CH3)3C+ much more stable.
